messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 69
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: South Eastern Asian
  relationship_status: Widowed
  occupation: Nanny
  trauma_type: Child's life-threatening illness
  pcl5: 71

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Maladaptive Strategies: Avoid Medical Care: Seeking medical or psychological help, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma, Mental Distraction: keep mind occupied all the time
  Memory: No Coherent Story: I cannot tell a clear story of what happened even to myself, More Real Than Normal: My memories of the event feel more real and vivid than memories of ordinary things, Feels Present Not Past: The memory feels like it is happening right now rather than something that is over
  Negative Appraisals: Unrecognisable Self: The person I have become is unrecognisable to me, Distrust Others: People are not what they seem, Permanent Damage: I have permanently changed for the worse

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

It was a Tuesday afternoon when Sophea’s three-year-old granddaughter, Maly, first began to cough. He had been watching her in the living room of his son’s house in Stockton, a glass of water in his hand, when the sound turned wet and sharp. Within hours, her fever spiked and her breathing grew labored. At the emergency room, the doctors spoke in rapid, clipped sentences he could not fully follow—sepsis, respiratory failure, pediatric intensive care. For seventeen days, Sophea sat in a vinyl chair by her bed, watching machines breathe for her, watching her small chest rise and fall in a rhythm that felt borrowed. He did not sleep. He did not eat. He held her hand and prayed to ancestors whose names he had not spoken aloud in years. When Maly finally opened her eyes and asked for a banana, the relief that washed over him was so complete it felt like a physical collapse. But something else had already taken root.

In the months that followed, Sophea found he could not hold the sequence of those seventeen days in his mind as a story with a beginning, middle, and end. If someone asked him what happened, he would open his mouth and find only fragments—the sound of a monitor alarm, the fluorescent glare of the hallway at 3 a.m., the weight of his son’s hand on his shoulder. He could not say how the doctors had explained the diagnosis, or what he had said to his daughter-in-law when she arrived. The pieces refused to assemble. And yet, at the same time, the memory did not feel distant or faded. It felt more real than anything around him. When he was pushing Maly on the swings at the park, the memory of the hospital room would suddenly press in on him with a vividness that made the playground dissolve. The beeping of the machines would fill his ears, and he would smell the antiseptic and the cold, recycled air. For a moment, he was there again, and the present—the grass, the sunshine, his granddaughter’s laughter—felt like a thin, unconvincing dream.

He began to avoid things. He stopped watching television because the news might show a child in a hospital bed. He refused to visit his own doctor for a routine blood pressure check, telling his son he felt fine. The thought of sitting in a waiting room, of seeing a stethoscope or an IV stand, filled him with a dread so immediate he could not explain it. He told himself the best thing was just to keep moving. He filled every hour of every day: cleaning the house, cooking elaborate meals, walking to the grocery store even when he did not need anything. He tried not to think about the hospital, and when the images came, he would force his mind onto something else—the price of eggs, the way the floorboards creaked, the list of chores for tomorrow. He kept his mind occupied all the time, because stillness was dangerous.

The person he had become was unrecognizable to him. Before Maly’s illness, Sophea had been a man who laughed easily, who stopped to chat with neighbors, who trusted that the world was basically predictable. Now he looked in the mirror and saw a stranger—a man who flinched at sudden noises, who watched people’s faces for signs of hidden danger. He had come to believe that people were not what they seemed. A friendly smile from a cashier felt like a mask; a kind word from his son felt like prelude to bad news. He was certain he had permanently changed for the worse. There was no going back to the person he had been, and that loss felt deeper than the fear itself.

His work as a nanny had once been a source of joy. He had cared for children his whole adult life, first his own, then others’. But now, every cough from a child sent a spike of terror through his chest. He found himself checking the children’s temperatures multiple times a day, listening to their breathing while they slept. He no longer took them to the park or to playdates, inventing excuses about traffic or weather. The parents noticed. They asked if he was feeling all right. He said he was fine, but he saw the doubt in their eyes. One family let him go gently, saying they needed someone with more energy. He did not argue. He told himself it was for the best.

What finally brought him to a clinic was his son’s quiet insistence. Sophea had stopped leaving the house except for essentials. He had lost twelve pounds. He could not remember the last time he had laughed. He sat in the intake room with his hands folded, unable to look the therapist in the eye. He said he did not know if talking could help. He said he was afraid that if he let himself remember, he would never stop. But he was also afraid of staying the way he was—afraid of disappearing into a life that felt like a waiting room, with no end in sight.
